event: Elsie wakes to the bread smell and hums the caravan song while she dresses.
She waters the plants and tells Doris the aloe all about Cora's eel bite.
Downstairs she buys honey buns for four, and the baker twists them up in paper.
At the guild hall Cora is already at the board, a fresh bandage under her cuff.
Elsie asks to see the bite, and Cora rolls back her cuff at once.
It is healing clean, Elsie says so, and Cora rolls the cuff down slowly.
Tamsin and Tilly come in together, arguing about whether eels have ears.
Elsie hands round the honey buns, Cora's first.
On the F-rank board are the glasshouse watch and the festival fireworks.
Tilly reads do not drop on the fireworks notice, and goes pale with joy.
Tamsin says they can do both: fireworks by day, orchids by night.
Elsie says that's two nearer E-rank, and Tilly bounces on her toes.
The clerk enters the party for both notices, and Cora writes them in her ledger.
Powder Lane smells of sulphur, and Tilly breathes it in like roses.
The firework maker, an old man with singed eyebrows, points them at four straw-packed crates.
Each crate is stencilled do not drop, and Tilly reads every one aloud.
Tilly asks him about his star mixes, and they talk powders while the others wait.
He gives Tilly a paper twist of his blue-star powder to try, and she holds it like a jewel.
Tamsin takes two crates; Elsie and Tilly carry one between them; Cora takes the last.
They carry the crates through the streets at a crawl, Tilly calling out every kerb.
A dog runs barking at Tamsin's legs, and she stands like a statue till it goes.
At the Lantern Steps a boatman rows them out over the Mere, crates between their knees.
The Mere is flat and shining, and Elsie trails her fingers in the water.
Tilly sits rigid with a crate in her lap and her eyes shut tight.
Elsie holds Tilly's elbow, and Tilly opens one eye and looks at her instead of the water.
The festival barge is half-built and hung with unlit lanterns, carpenters hammering.
The barge master counts the crates aboard, every one whole, and pays them the notice.
Elsie, Tamsin and Tilly share it, and Elsie gives Tilly the odd pips.
The barge master says Midsummer Lantern Night is on the twentieth, and they should come.
He says the whole Mere fills with lantern boats, and fireworks burst over them.
Elsie turns to the others with shining eyes, and Tamsin says they're coming, all of them.
Cora says she'll be on duty; Elsie says then she'll be on duty in a boat, with them.
Back on the Lantern Steps, Tilly kneels and pats the stone, and the boatman laughs.
At the Tipsy Heron Elsie pays for a pot of tea for four, and they share the last buns.
Cora says the glasshouse watch starts at dusk, and they should sleep this afternoon.
Tilly says she can never sleep in the day; Tamsin says watch her.
Cora goes to the Wardens' room to write, and says she'll meet them at the glasshouse gate.
Tamsin stretches out on the Heron's back bench and is asleep in a breath; they leave her there.
Tilly asks to nap in Elsie's attic, since her own room smells of sulphur.
The attic bed is narrow, and Tilly lies stiff as a board on the very edge.
Elsie says she'll fall out, pulls her in, and tucks a singed braid behind her ear.
Tilly lies very still, looking at the sloped ceiling and breathing carefully.
Elsie falls asleep in moments, one arm thrown over Tilly's waist.
Elsie wakes to find Tilly awake and watching her, and Tilly goes scarlet.
Tilly says she counted the boards in the ceiling, all of them, twice.
They eat bread and cheese at the round window, and Elsie packs salve and bandages.
At sunset they walk the lake road to a walled garden with a long white glasshouse.
Tamsin and Cora wait at the garden gate with the old grower.
The grower says her moon orchids open at moonrise tonight, one night in the year.
She says thieves come over the wall for them, and lamp moths as big as a hand bruise the petals.
She shows them a stove, a kettle and one narrow cot for the watch, and goes up to her house.
Inside, the glasshouse is long and warm, row on row of closed buds on dark leaves.
Tamsin sets herself at the door with Margery; Cora takes the wall side, ledger out.
Tilly lines up vials on the potting bench and says she will finish her smoke tonight.
The moon comes up over the wall, and the buds begin to open, one after another.
The moon orchids glow silver all down the glasshouse, and Elsie's eyes fill.
Cora stands beside her, looking at the flowers, then at Elsie's face in their light.
Lamp moths come out of the dark, soft and hand-sized, and bump against the glass.
Some get in at the vents and settle on the orchids, bruising the petals brown.
Elsie catches one gently in cupped hands and carries it out to the garden.
Tamsin tries the same and squashes one, and looks so sorry that Elsie laughs.
Tilly's smoke curls off a vial, pale and lemony, and the moths drift away from it.
Wherever the smoke reaches the moths leave the orchids be; Tilly stares, then squeals.
Elsie hugs her off her feet, and Tilly says it's finished, her smoke is finished.
Something scrapes on the garden wall, and Tamsin says, quiet, company.
Two shapes drop over the wall and creep toward the glasshouse with sacks.
Tamsin steps out with Margery on her shoulder, and one thief bolts back over the wall.
The other trips in a bed of lettuces, and Elsie reaches her first.
She is a thin young woman in a patched coat, crying with fright.
She says her little brother has a fever, and a moon orchid would pay the apothecary.
Elsie tells her moonbells brew for fever, and sends her to the apothecary on Mortar Lane.
Elsie gives her bread from the satchel, and pays her coin for a fever draught from her own purse.
Cora watches, writes, and lets her go.
The young woman goes back over the wall with the bread held to her chest.
Tilly makes tea on the stove, and they drink it among the glowing orchids.
Tamsin takes the first sleep on the narrow cot with Margery across her chest, snoring.
Cora walks the wall; Elsie and Tilly sit on an upturned bucket and a crate, watching.
Tilly asks, very quietly, whether what she feels around Elsie could be the class.
She says she can't tell any more what is hers.
Elsie says she has never once used her class to make anyone feel anything.
Cora, at the door, says the ledger agrees: Tether, once, on Tamsin, by her leave.
Tilly looks down at her hands and says, in a very small voice, then it's mine.
Elsie says of course it's hers, whatever it is, and takes her hand.
Tilly holds Elsie's hand in both of hers, looks at the orchids, and keeps what it is to herself.
A lamp moth lands on Elsie's hair clip, glowing faintly, and Tilly laughs and coaxes it off.
